title: Joint prehabilitation with exercise and protein
official: Multimodal prehabilitation for frail patients undergoing total hip or knee replacement: The Joint PREP randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Hip and knee replacements are common operations. Some people having joint replacement are physically vulnerable to health setbacks. This is also called frailty. Exercise and a high protein diet can help people who are physically vulnerable. We know that exercise and a high protein diet can improve mobility and reduce complications after different types of surgery. However, we do not know how best to support physically vulnerable people having joint replacement. We want to see if daily home-based exercise and a high protein diet before surgery can help physically vulnerable patients having joint replacement.
We have completed a small study to see if the exercise and protein programme was acceptable to patients. Based on findings from this study, we made changes to the exercise programme to provide easier exercises.
We want to find out if home-based exercise and a high protein diet before surgery can help physically vulnerable patients having joint replacement.

Who can participate?
Physically vulnerable patients (based on responses to a screening questionnaire), aged 65 years or over, who have been placed on a waiting list for a hip or knee replacement and can safely exercise at home and eat extra protein.

What does the study involve?
We will involve 488 patients who are physically vulnerable having hip or knee replacement at up to 20 NHS hospitals. Patients will randomly be put into two groups with 244 patients in each group. Everyone in the study will have an equal chance of being in either group. We do this so that we can fairly compare the different treatments.
Patients in both groups will receive their usual hospital care. One group of patients will also have the extra Joint PREP exercise and protein programme. Joint PREP stands for Joint PRehabilitation with Exercise and Protein. This programme starts two to eight weeks after being put on the waiting list for joint replacement and continues until surgery.
Patients will have an appointment with a physiotherapist to design a personalised home exercise plan. Patients will be asked to follow this home exercise plan every day until surgery. To help build muscle strength, patients will also be given a daily protein supplement. This will be a jelly pot or a protein shake. Exercises and information will be provided on paper and an online platform.
Patients will be supported in the first 10 weeks of the Joint PREP programme by regular telephone or videocalls from a physiotherapist, followed by monthly information leaflets. Patients will also receive a follow-up call from a physiotherapist when they are given a surgery date to continue to encourage patients to do the prehabilitation programme in the weeks before surgery.
We will ask all patients in the study about their health up to 6 months after their operation. We will compare people’s answers in the two groups to find out if the Joint PREP programme is better than usual care. The main outcomes will be mobility and how many days people spend in hospital up to 6 months following surgery.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participating in the study may help to improve post operative recovery of physically vulnerable patients. There is no known direct benefit to taking part; however, some patients find taking part in a study rewarding and like the contact with research staff and having the opportunity to share experiences and opinions of their condition and treatment.
Risks for all participants could involve participating in the study for an unknown length of time due to the long surgical waiting lists in some hospitals, being asked to complete several questionnaires before and after surgery that could take between 30 to 45 minutes to complete each time and could cause some emotional distress because of the content, and potentially being at additional risk of breaches to data privacy because of the additional need to collect research data on separate systems to those used standard care.
Additional risks to participants who are randomised to the Joint PREP exercise and protein programme intervention group include attending a 1 hour appointment, although travel expenses are available to help with transport costs to this appointment in hospital, possibly experiencing some minor side effects of exercise including temporary ache in muscles and joints, or when taking the protein supplement a food intolerance is possible.

Where is the study run from?
The Sponsor of the study is Bristol NHS Foundation Trust and the coordinating centre running the study is Bristol Trials Centre at the University of Bristol (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to February 2029.

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research; Health Technology Assessment Programme (NIHR HTA reference 171964).

Who is the main contact?
The Joint PREP team at Bristol Trials Centre, jointprep-study@bristol.ac.uk

interventions.name:
The intervention which is called the 'Joint PREP programme' involves participants completing a home-based exercise programme (based on the participants ability) and consuming a protein supplement (a jelly pot or protein powder in the form of a shake) from randomisation until surgery.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Patients newly placed on the surgical waiting list for primary elective Total Hip Replacement (THR) or Total Knee Replacement (TKR)
2. Planned THR/TKR is either unilateral, or staged bilateral with the second procedure planned for more than 6 months after the first
3. >=65 years of age
4. Frail, defined as a self-reported Groningen Frailty Indicator (GFI) score of > = 4, an accepted threshold for identifying frailty
5. Expected surgical wait of >=12 weeks*, to allow patients a minimum duration of exercise that is likely to have benefits to frailty 
*If the expected wait is <12 weeks, patients are eligible to be approached if processes are in place at the site that would allow a patient the opportunity to participate in 12 weeks of the intervention prior to their surgery, with the patient's agreement
Exclusion criteria:
1. Contraindications to study intervention - following a low protein diet or co-morbidities which preclude safe participation in physical exercise e.g. severe aortic stenosis, unstable angina, uncontrolled arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, accelerated hypertension >200mmHg or myocarditis. This will be assessed on a case-by-case basis by the local PI, and if needed through consultation with the Clinical Lead and Intervention Leads**
2. Listed for simultaneous bilateral Total Hip Replacement (THR) or Total Knee Replacement (TKR)
3. Co-enrolment in a study in which participation in another trial is not permitted
4. Unable or unwilling to provide informed consent, as assessed by the clinical care team
5. Previously enrolled in the study 
**There are very few absolute contraindications to consuming protein supplements. Similarly there are very few absolute contraindications to physical activity and most of these would likely preclude elective surgery. Therefore, on that basis, we anticipate most people who are being considered for elective joint replacement would be able to undertake some physical activity
